reconcile.connective: Commentators read Genesis 1:29's universal grant as already carrying the single exception that Genesis 2:17 then names — all trees but one.

discrepancy.connective: Source critics such as Richard Elliott Friedman press the objection that Genesis 1 (P) and Genesis 2 (J) are two originally separate accounts, so the unrestricted food grant and the lone prohibition reflect different authors rather than one coherent rule.

skeptic.name: Richard Elliott Friedman
skeptic.attribution: Richard Elliott Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible? (1987)

excerpts.excerpt_text: all but the tree of knowledge, of good and evil, afterwards excepted … and the various fruits of all sorts of trees, but that before mentioned
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill reads the 'every tree' of 1:29 as itself excepting the tree of knowledge that 2:17 forbids — the core harmonization that the universal grant already presupposes the one exception.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Of every tree in the garden thou mayest freely eat. … But of the other tree which stood very near the tree of life (for they are both said to be in the midst of the garden), and which was called the tree of knowledge, in the day thou eatest thereof, thou shalt surely die …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry frames the generous grant ('of every tree... freely eat') and the single excepted tree as one coherent arrangement, not two conflicting rules — the grant and the prohibition stand together.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Genesis 1:29
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, reading the 'every tree' grant of 1:29 as already excepting the tree of knowledge prohibited in 2:17.
